title: Chapter 14 — Taste For Physical Gratifications United In America To Love Of Freedom And Attention To Public Affairs
paragraphs: Of Freedom And Attention To Public Affairs

When a democratic state turns into an absolute monarchy, the activity that was previously directed toward public as well as private affairs is suddenly concentrated on private affairs alone. The immediate consequence, for a time, is great physical prosperity. But the impulse soon slackens, and the level of productive industry begins to stall. I do not know whether a single trading or manufacturing people can be named — from the Tyrians down to the Florentines and the English — that was not also a free people. There is therefore a close bond and a necessary relation between these two elements: freedom and productive industry. This is generally true of all nations, but especially of democratic nations. I have already shown that men who live in ages of equality continually need to form associations in order to obtain the things they want. And I have also shown how greatly political freedom improves and spreads the art of association. In such ages freedom is therefore especially favorable to the production of wealth. It is not hard to see that despotism is especially hostile to that result. The nature of despotic power in democratic ages is not to be fierce or cruel, but minute and meddling. Despotism of this kind, though it does not trample on humanity, stands directly opposed to the spirit of commerce and the pursuits of industry.

So men of democratic ages need to be free in order to obtain more readily those physical enjoyments they are always longing for. It sometimes happens, however, that the excessive taste they develop for those same enjoyments hands them over to the first master who appears. The passion for worldly welfare then defeats itself and, without their noticing, pushes the very object of their desires further away.

There is, indeed, a most dangerous passage in the history of a democratic people. When the taste for physical gratification among such a people has grown faster than its education and its experience of free institutions, a time comes when men are carried away and lose all self-restraint at the sight of the new possessions they are about to seize. In their intense and exclusive anxiety to make a fortune, they lose sight of the close connection between the private fortune of each and the prosperity of all. It is not necessary to use violence against such a people in order to strip them of the rights they enjoy; they themselves willingly let go. The performance of political duties seems to them a troublesome annoyance that diverts them from their occupations and business. If they are required to elect representatives, to support the government by personal service, to gather for public business, they have no time — they cannot waste their precious time on useless engagements. Such idle pursuits are unsuited to serious men engaged in the more important interests of life. These people think they are following the principle of self-interest, but the idea they have of that principle is a very crude one. In order to look after what they call their business, they neglect their chief business, which is to remain their own masters.

Since the citizens who work do not care to attend to public business, and since the class that might devote its leisure to these duties has ceased to exist, the place of government is, as it were, left vacant. If at that critical moment some able and ambitious man seizes supreme power, he will find the road to every kind of usurpation open before him. If he attends for a while to the material prosperity of the country, nothing more will be required of him. Above all, he must guarantee public tranquility. Men possessed by the passion for physical gratification generally discover that the turmoil of freedom disturbs their well-being before they discover how freedom itself actually promotes it. If the slightest rumor of public commotion intrudes on the petty pleasures of their private lives, they are stirred and alarmed by it. The fear of anarchy perpetually haunts them, and they are always ready to throw away their freedom at the first disturbance.

I readily admit that public tranquility is a great good. But at the same time I cannot forget that all nations have been enslaved by being kept in good order. Certainly this is not to suggest that nations should despise public tranquility. But that state of affairs should not be enough for them. A nation that asks nothing of its government except the maintenance of order is already a slave at heart — the slave of its own well-being, waiting only for the hand that will bind it. By such a nation the despotism of a faction is no less to be feared than the despotism of an individual. When the bulk of the community is absorbed by private concerns, the smallest parties need not despair of gaining the upper hand in public affairs. At such times it is not rare to see, upon the great stage of the world, what we see at our theaters — a multitude represented by a few actors, who alone speak in the name of an absent or inattentive crowd. They alone are in motion while all the rest are still; they regulate everything by their own whim; they change the laws and tyrannize at will over the customs of the country. Then men are astonished to see into how small a number of weak and worthless hands a great people can fall.

Up to now the Americans have fortunately escaped all the dangers I have just described, and in this respect they truly deserve admiration. Perhaps there is no country in the world where fewer idle men are to be found than in America, or where those who work are more eager to promote their own welfare. But if the Americans' passion for physical gratifications is intense, at least it is not undiscriminating; and reason, though unable to restrain it, still guides its course. An American attends to his private concerns as if he were alone in the world, and the next minute he gives himself up to the common good as if he had forgotten them. At one moment he seems driven by the most selfish greed, at another by the most lively patriotism. The human heart cannot really be split in two. The inhabitants of the United States display so strong and so similar a passion for their own welfare and for their freedom, by turns, that one must suppose these passions are united and blended somewhere in their character. And indeed the Americans believe their freedom to be the best instrument and the surest safeguard of their welfare. They are attached to the one through the other. They by no means think they are not called to take part in the public good. On the contrary, they believe their chief business is to secure for themselves a government that will allow them to obtain the things they want and will not bar them from the peaceful enjoyment of the possessions they have acquired.
